1 INTRODUCTION: Population of neurons, especially in higher-order perceptual and motor cortices, show coordinated pattern of activity constrained to an approximately low dimensional ‘neural manifold’ (Sohn et al., 2019; Churchland et al., 2012; Saxena et al., 2022). The dynamical structure of latent trajectories evolving along the neural manifold is thought to be a valid substrate of neural computation. This idea has fostered extensive experimental studies and the development of computational methods to extract these trajectories directly from electrophysiological recordings. Great strides have been made in developing computational tools for the purpose of extracting latent neural trajectories in post hoc neural data analysis. However, while recently developed tools have proven their efficacy in accurately inferring latent neural trajectories (Pandarinath et al., 2018; Pei et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2009; Zhao & Park, 2017), learning their underlying dynamics has received markedly less attention. Furthermore, even less focus has been placed on real-time methods that allow for online learning of neural trajectories and their underlying dynamics. Real time learning of neural dynamics would facilitate more efficient experimental design, and increase the capability of closed-loop systems where an accurate picture of the dynamical landscape leads to more precise predictions (Peixoto et al., 2021; Bolus et al., 2021). In this work, we consider the problem of inferring latent trajectories while simultaneously learning the dynamical system generating them in an online fashion. We introduce the exponential family variational Kalman filter (eVKF), a novel variational inference scheme that draws inspiration from the ‘predict’ and ‘update’ steps used in the classic Kalman filter (Anderson & Moore, 1979). We theoretically justify our variational inference scheme by proving it leads to a tighter ‘filtering’ evidence lower bound (ELBO) than a ‘single step’ approximation that utilizes the closed form solution of the proposed ‘variational prediction’ step. Finally, we show how parameterization of the dynamics via a universal function approximator in tandem with exponential family properties facilitates an alternative optimization procedure for learning the generative model. Our contributions are as follows: (i) We propose a novel variational inference scheme for online learning analogous to the predict and update steps of the Kalman filter. (ii) We show the variational prediction step offers a closed form solution when we restrict our variational approximations to constant base measure exponential families (Theorem 1). (iii) We justify our two step procedure by showing that we achieve a tighter bound on the ELBO, when compared to directly finding a variational approximation to the filtering distribution (Theorem 2). (iv) We show that when using universal function approximators for modeling the dynamics, we can optimize our model of the dynamics without propagating gradients through the ELBO as is typically done in variational expectation maximization (vEM) or variational autoencoders (VAEs) (Kingma & Welling, 2014). 2 BACKGROUND:  2.1 STATE-SPACE MODELS: In this paper, we consider observations (e.g. neural recordings), yt, arriving in a sequential fashion. It is assumed these observations depend directly on a latent Markov process (e.g. structured neural dynamics), zt, allowing us to write the generative model in state-space form: zt | zt−1 ∼ pθ(zt | zt−1) (latent dynamics model) yt | zt ∼ pψ(yt | zt) (observation model) where zt ∈ RL, yt ∈ RN , ψ parameterize the observation model, and θ parameterize the dynamics model. After observing yt, any statistical quantities of interest related to zt can be computed from the filtering distribution, p(zt | y1:t). Since we are considering a periodically sampled data streaming setting, it is important that we are able to compute p(zt | y1:t) in a recursive fashion, with constant time and space complexity. In addition to inferring the filtering distribution over latent states, we will also be interested in learning the dynamics as (prior) conditional probability distribution, given by pθ(zt | zt−1), that captures the underlying dynamical law that governs the latent state z and may implement neural computation. Learning the dynamics facilitates higher quality inference of the latent state, accurate forecasting, and generation of new data. In this paper we will be focused mainly on models where the dynamics are non-linear and parameterized by flexible function approximators. For example, we may model the dynamics as zt | zt−1 ∼ N (fθ(zt−1),Q), with an arbitrary function approximator fθ : RL → RL such as neural networks. 2.2 KALMAN FILTER: Before diving into the general case, let’s revisit the well-established Kalman filter (Särkkä, 2013). Given linear Gaussian dynamics and observations, the state-space model description is given by pθ(zt | zt−1) = N (zt | Azt−1,Q) pψ(yt | zt) = N (yt | Czt + b,R) θ = {A,Q} ψ = {C,b,R} The Kalman filter recursively computes the Bayes optimal estimate of the latent state zt. Given the filtering posterior of previous time step, p(zt−1 | y1:t−1) = N (mt−1,Pt−1), we first predict the latent state distribution (a.k.a. the filtering prior) at time t p̄(zt | y1:t−1) = Ep(zt−1|y1:t−1) pθ(zt | zt−1) (1) = N (zt | Amt−1,APt−1A> + Q) (2) Secondly, we update our belief of the current state with the observation yt by Bayes’ rule p(zt | y1:t) ∝ p(yt | zt) p̄(zt | y1:t−1) (3) = N (zt |mt,Pt) (4) In order to learn the underlying dynamics A, the linear readout C, state noise Q and observation noise R, the EM algorithm can be employed (Ghahramani & Hinton, 1996). If a calibrated measure of uncertainty over the model parameters is important, then a prior can be placed over those quantities, and approximate Bayesian methods can be used to find the posterior (Barber & Chiappa, 2006). Note that these methods are for learning the parameters in the offline setting. 3 EXPONENTIAL FAMILY VARIATIONAL KALMAN FILTER (EVKF): When the models are not linear and Gaussian, the filtering prior Eq. 1 INTRODUCTION: Population of neurons, especially in higher-order perceptual and motor cortices, show coordinated pattern of activity constrained to an approximately low dimensional ‘neural manifold’ (Sohn et al., 2019; Churchland et al., 2012; Saxena et al., 2022). The dynamical structure of latent trajectories evolving along the neural manifold is thought to be a valid substrate of neural computation. This idea has fostered extensive experimental studies and the development of computational methods to extract these trajectories directly from electrophysiological recordings. Great strides have been made in developing computational tools for the purpose of extracting latent neural trajectories in post hoc neural data analysis. However, while recently developed tools have proven their efficacy in accurately inferring latent neural trajectories (Pandarinath et al., 2018; Pei et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2009; Zhao & Park, 2017), learning their underlying dynamics has received markedly less attention. Furthermore, even less focus has been placed on real-time methods that allow for online learning of neural trajectories and their underlying dynamics. Real time learning of neural dynamics would facilitate more efficient experimental design, and increase the capability of closed-loop systems where an accurate picture of the dynamical landscape leads to more precise predictions (Peixoto et al., 2021; Bolus et al., 2021). In this work, we consider the problem of inferring latent trajectories while simultaneously learning the dynamical system generating them in an online fashion. We introduce the exponential family variational Kalman filter (eVKF), a novel variational inference scheme that draws inspiration from the ‘predict’ and ‘update’ steps used in the classic Kalman filter (Anderson & Moore, 1979). We theoretically justify our variational inference scheme by proving it leads to a tighter ‘filtering’ evidence lower bound (ELBO) than a ‘single step’ approximation that utilizes the closed form solution of the proposed ‘variational prediction’ step. Finally, we show how parameterization of the dynamics via a universal function approximator in tandem with exponential family properties facilitates an alternative optimization procedure for learning the generative model. Our contributions are as follows: (i) We propose a novel variational inference scheme for online learning analogous to the predict and update steps of the Kalman filter. (ii) We show the variational prediction step offers a closed form solution when we restrict our variational approximations to constant base measure exponential families (Theorem 1). (iii) We justify our two step procedure by showing that we achieve a tighter bound on the ELBO, when compared to directly finding a variational approximation to the filtering distribution (Theorem 2). (iv) We show that when using universal function approximators for modeling the dynamics, we can optimize our model of the dynamics without propagating gradients through the ELBO as is typically done in variational expectation maximization (vEM) or variational autoencoders (VAEs) (Kingma & Welling, 2014). 2 BACKGROUND:  2.1 STATE-SPACE MODELS: In this paper, we consider observations (e.g. neural recordings), yt, arriving in a sequential fashion. It is assumed these observations depend directly on a latent Markov process (e.g. structured neural dynamics), zt, allowing us to write the generative model in state-space form: zt | zt−1 ∼ pθ(zt | zt−1) (latent dynamics model) yt | zt ∼ pψ(yt | zt) (observation model) where zt ∈ RL, yt ∈ RN , ψ parameterize the observation model, and θ parameterize the dynamics model. After observing yt, any statistical quantities of interest related to zt can be computed from the filtering distribution, p(zt | y1:t). Since we are considering a periodically sampled data streaming setting, it is important that we are able to compute p(zt | y1:t) in a recursive fashion, with constant time and space complexity. In addition to inferring the filtering distribution over latent states, we will also be interested in learning the dynamics as (prior) conditional probability distribution, given by pθ(zt | zt−1), that captures the underlying dynamical law that governs the latent state z and may implement neural computation. Learning the dynamics facilitates higher quality inference of the latent state, accurate forecasting, and generation of new data. In this paper we will be focused mainly on models where the dynamics are non-linear and parameterized by flexible function approximators. For example, we may model the dynamics as zt | zt−1 ∼ N (fθ(zt−1),Q), with an arbitrary function approximator fθ : RL → RL such as neural networks. 2.2 KALMAN FILTER: Before diving into the general case, let’s revisit the well-established Kalman filter (Särkkä, 2013). Given linear Gaussian dynamics and observations, the state-space model description is given by pθ(zt | zt−1) = N (zt | Azt−1,Q) pψ(yt | zt) = N (yt | Czt + b,R) θ = {A,Q} ψ = {C,b,R} The Kalman filter recursively computes the Bayes optimal estimate of the latent state zt. Given the filtering posterior of previous time step, p(zt−1 | y1:t−1) = N (mt−1,Pt−1), we first predict the latent state distribution (a.k.a. the filtering prior) at time t p̄(zt | y1:t−1) = Ep(zt−1|y1:t−1) pθ(zt | zt−1) (1) = N (zt | Amt−1,APt−1A> + Q) (2) Secondly, we update our belief of the current state with the observation yt by Bayes’ rule p(zt | y1:t) ∝ p(yt | zt) p̄(zt | y1:t−1) (3) = N (zt |mt,Pt) (4) In order to learn the underlying dynamics A, the linear readout C, state noise Q and observation noise R, the EM algorithm can be employed (Ghahramani & Hinton, 1996). If a calibrated measure of uncertainty over the model parameters is important, then a prior can be placed over those quantities, and approximate Bayesian methods can be used to find the posterior (Barber & Chiappa, 2006). Note that these methods are for learning the parameters in the offline setting. 3 EXPONENTIAL FAMILY VARIATIONAL KALMAN FILTER (EVKF): When the models are not linear and Gaussian, the filtering prior Eq. (1) and filtering distribution Eq. (3) are often intractable. This is unfortunate since most models of practical interests deviate in one way or another from these linear Gaussian assumptions. Drawing inspiration from the predict and update procedure for recursive Bayesian estimation, we propose the exponential family variational Kalman filter (eVKF), a recursive variational inference procedure for exponential family models that jointly infers latent trajectories and learns their underlying dynamics. 3.1 EXPONENTIAL FAMILY DISTRIBUTIONS: We first take time to recall exponential family distributions, as their theoretical properties make them convenient to work with, especially when performing Bayesian inference. An exponential family distribution can be written as p(z) = h(z) exp ( λ>t(z)−A(λ) ) (5) where h(z) is the base measure, λ is the natural parameter, t(z) is the sufficient statistics, and A(λ) is the log-partition function (Wainwright & Jordan, 2008). Many widely used distributions reside in the exponential family; a Gaussian distribution, p(z) = N (m,P), for example, has t(z) = [ z zz> ] , λ = [ − 12P −1m − 12P −1] and h(z) = (2π)−L/2. Note that the base measure h does not depend on z for a Gaussian distribution. We hereby call such an exponential family distribution a constant base measure if its base measure, h, is constant w.r.t. z. This class encapsulates many well known distributions such as the Gaussian, Bernoulli, Beta, and Gamma distributions. An additional and important fact we use is that, for a minimal1 exponential family distribution, there exists a one-to-one mapping between the natural parameters, λ, and the mean parameters, µ := Ep(z)t(z). This mapping is given by µ = ∇λA(λ), and its inverse by λ = ∇µEp(z;λ(µ)) log p(z;λ(µ)), though Ep(z;λ(µ)) log p(z;λ(µ)) is usually intractable (Seeger, 2005). If we have a conditional exponential family distribution, pθ(zt | zt−1), then the natural parameters of zt | zt−1 are a function of zt−1. In this case, we can write the conditional density function as pθ(zt | zt−1) = h(zt) exp(λθ(zt−1)>t(zt)−A(λθ(zt−1))) (6) where λθ(·) maps zt−1 to the space of valid natural parameters for zt. This allows us to use expressive natural parameter mappings, while keeping the conditional distribution in the constant base measure exponential family. Assume that at time t, we have an approximation to the filtering distribution, q(zt−1), and that this approximation is a constant base measure exponential family distribution so that p(zt−1 | y1:t−1) ≈ q(zt−1) = h exp(λ>t(zt−1)−A(λ)) (7) The primary goal of filtering is to efficiently compute a good approximation q(zt) of p(xt | y1:t), the filtering distribution at time t. As we will show, following the prescription of two-step variational procedure, predict and then update, leads to a natural variational inference scheme and a provably tighter ELBO than the typical single-step variational approximation. 3.2 VARIATIONAL PREDICTION STEP: Now that we have relaxed the linear Gaussian assumption, the first problem we encounter is computing the predictive distribution (a.k.a. filtering prior) p̄(zt | y1:t−1) = Ep(zt−1|y1:t−1)pθ(zt | zt−1) (8) This is generally intractable, since the filtering distribution, p(zt−1 | y1:t−1), can only be found analytically for simple SSMs. Similar to other online variational methods (Marino et al., 2018; Zhao & Park, 2020; Campbell et al., 2021), we subsitute an approximation for the filtering distribution, q(zt−1) ≈ p(zt−1 | y1:t−1), and consider Eq(zt−1)pθ(zt | zt−1) (9) Unfortunately, due to the nonlinearity in pθ(zt | zt−1), Eq. (9) is still intractable, making further approximation necessary. We begin by considering an approximation, q̄(zt), restricted to a minimal exponential family distribution with natural parameter λ̄, i.e. Eq(zt−1)pθ(zt | zt−1) ≈ q̄(zt) = h exp(λ̄ >t(zt)−A(λ̄)) (10) 1minimality means that all sufficient statistics are linearly independent. Taking a variational approach (Hoffman et al., 2013), our goal is to find the natural parameter λ̄ that minimizes DKL ( q̄(zt)||Eq(zt−1)pθ(zt | zt−1) ) . Since this quantity cannot be minimized directly, we can consider the following upper bound: F = −H(q̄(zt))− Eq̄(zt)Eq(zt−1) log pθ(zt | zt−1) (11) ≥ DKL ( q̄(zt)||Eq(zt−1)p(zt | zt−1) ) (12) Rather than minimizing F with respect to λ̄ through numerical optimization, if we take q(zt−1), q̄(zt), and pθ(zt | zt−1) to be in the same constant base measure exponential family, then we can show the following theorem which tells us how to compute the λ̄ ∗ that minimizes F . Theorem 1 (Variational prediction distribution). If pθ(zt | zt−1), q(zt), and q̄(zt) are chosen to be in the same minimal and constant base measure exponential family distribution, Ec, then q̄ ∗(zt) = argminq̄∈Ec F(q̄) has a closed form solution given by q̄ ∗(zt) with natural parameters, λ̄θ λ̄θ = Eq(zt−1)λθ(zt−1) (13) Eq. (13) demonstrates that the optimal natural parameters of q̄ are the expected natural parameters of the prior dynamics under the variational filtering posterior. While λ̄θ cannot be found analytically, computing a Monte-Carlo approximation is simple; we only have to draw samples from q(zt−1) and then pass those samples through λθ(·). This also reveals a very nice symmetry that exists between closed form conjugate Bayesian updates and variationally inferring the prediction distribution. In the former case we calculate Eq(zt−1)pθ(zt | zt−1) while in the latter we calculate Eq(zt−1)λθ(zt−1). We summarize the eVKF two-step procedure in Algorithm 1, located in Appendix D.3. 3.3 VARIATIONAL UPDATE STEP: Analogous to the Kalman filter, we update our belief of the latent state after observing yt. When the likelihood is conjugate to the filtering prior, we can calculate a Bayesian update in closed form by using q̄(zt) as our prior and computing p(zt | y1:t) ≈ q(zt) ∝ p(yt | zt)q̄(zt) where q(zt), with natural parameter λ, belongs to the same family as q(zt−1). In the absence of conjugacy, we use variational inference to find q(zt) by maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO) λ∗ = argmax λ Lt(λ,θ) (14) = argmax λ [ Eq(zt) log p(yt | zt)− DKL(q(zt | λ)||q̄(zt)) ] (15) If the likelihood happens to be an exponential family family distribution, then one way to maximize Eq. (14) is through conjugate computation variational inference (CVI) (Khan & Lin, 2017). CVI is appealing in this case because it is equivalent to natural gradient descent, and thus converges faster, and conveniently it operates in the natural parameter space that we are already working in. 3.4 TIGHT LOWER BOUND BY THE PREDICT-UPDATE PROCEDURE: A natural alternative to the variational predict then update procedure prescribed is to directly find a variational approximation to the filtering distribution. One way is to substitute Eq(zt−1)pθ(zt | zt−1) for q̄(zt) into the ELBO earlier (Marino et al., 2018; Zhao & Park, 2020). Further details are provided in Appendix B, but after making this substitution and invoking Jensen’s inequality we get the following lower bound on the log-marginal likelihood at time t Mt = Eq(zt) log p(yt | zt)− Eq(zt) [ log q(zt)− Eq(zt−1) log p(zt | zt−1) ] (16) However, as we prove in Appendix B, this leads to a provably looser bound on the evidence compared to eVKF, as we state in the following theorem. Theorem 2 (Tightness of Lt). If we set ∆(q) = Lt(q)−Mt(q) (17) then, we have that ∆(q) = Eq(zt−1)A(λθ(zt−1))−A(λ̄θ) ≥ 0. (18) In other words, the bound on the evidence when using the variational predict then update procedure is always tighter than the one step procedure. Thus, not only do the variational predict then update steps simplify computations, and make leveraging conjugacy possible, they also facilitate a better approximation to the posterior filtering distribution. 3.5 LEARNING THE DYNAMICS: Our remaining desiderata is the ability to learn the parameters of the dynamics model pθ(zt | zt−1). One way of learning θ, is to use variational expectation maximization; with λ∗ fixed, we find the θ∗ that maximizes the ELBO θ∗ = argmax θ L(λ∗,θ) (19) = argmin θ DKL ( q(zt;λ ∗)||q̄θ(zt; λ̄θ) ) (20) This objective may require expensive computation in practice, e.g. the log-determinant and Cholesky decomposition for Gaussian q and q̄θ . However, since we chose q̄θ and q to be in the same exponential family, then as described in the following Proposition, we can consider the more computationally tracktable square loss function as an optimization objective. Proposition 1 (Optimal θ). If the mapping from zt−1 to the natural parameters of zt, given by λθ(zt−1), is a universal function approximator with trainable parameters, θ, then setting θ∗ = argmin θ 1 2 ||λ ∗ − λ̄θ||2 (21) is equivalent to finding θ∗ = argmaxθ Lt(λ∗,θ). The proposition indicates that we find the optimal θ∗ that matches the natural parameters of predictive distribution to that of the filtering distribution. The proof can be found in Appendix C. Empirically, we have found that even for small neural networks, following Eq. (21), works better in practice than directly minimizing the KL term. 3.6 CORRECTING FOR THE UNDERESTIMATION OF VARIANCE: It might be illuminating to take a linear and Gaussian dynamical system, and compare the variational approximation of eVKF to the closed form solutions given by Kalman filtering. Given pθ(zt | zt−1) = N (zt | Azt−1,Q), the mapping from a realization of zt−1 to the natural parameters of zt is given by λθ(zt−1) = [ − 12Q −1Azt−1 − 12 vec(Q −1) ] . With this mapping, we can determine in closed form the prediction distribution given by eVKF. Assuming that q(zt−1) = N (zt−1 | mt−1,Pt−1), we can find the optimal variational prediction distribution by plugging λθ(zt−1), into Eq. (13) to find q̄(zt) = N (zt | Amt−1,Q) (22) However, we know that the prediction step of the Kalman filter returns p̄(zt) = N (zt | Amt−1,Q + APt−1A>) (23) Though this issue has been examined when applying VI to time series models, as in Turner & Sahani (2011), it demonstrates that eVKF underestimates the true variance by an amount APt−1A>. For this example, we see that because the second natural parameter does not depend on at least second order moments of zt−1, the uncertainty provided by Pt−1 will not be propagated forward. At least for the linear and Gaussian case, we can correct this with a post-hoc fix by adding APt−1A> to the variance of the variational prediction. If we consider nonlinear Gaussian dynamics with pθ(zt | zt−1) = N (zt |mθ(zt−1),Q), then there does not exist an exact correction since the true prediction distribution will not be Gaussian. Empirically, we have found that adding an extended Kalman filter (Särkkä, 2013) like correction of Mt−1Pt−1M>t−1 to the prediction distribution variance, where Mt−1 = ∇mθ(mt−1), helps to avoid overconfidence. In the Appendix D.4 we show a case where not including an additional variance term gives unsatisfactory results when dynamical transitions are Gamma distributed. 4 RELATED WORKS: Classic recursive Bayesian methods such as the particle filter (PF), extended Kalman filter (EKF), and unscented Kalman filter (UKF) are widely used for online state-estimation (Särkkä, 2013). Typically, these methods assume a known generative model, but unknown parameters can also be learned by including them through expectation maximization (EM), or dual filtering (Haykin, 2002; Wan & Van Der Merwe, 2000; Wan & Nelson, 1997). While the PF can be used to learn the parameters of the dynamics in an online fashion, as in Kantas et al. (2015), it suffers from the well known issue of “weight degeneracy” limiting its applicability to low dimensional systems. While methods from the subspace identification literature are frequently employed to estimate the underlying dynamics in an offline setting, they are often limited to linear systems (Buesing et al., 2012). Marino et al. (2018) and Zhao & Park (2020)(VJF), in contrast to eVKF, perform a single step approximation each time instant. Zhao et al. (2022)(SVMC) use particle filtering to infer the filtering distribution and derives a surrogate ELBO for parameter learning. Campbell et al. (2021)(OVS) use a factorized approximate joint posterior. Note that it updates the second most recent state with the most recent observation so that it is technically smoothing rather than filtering. 5 EXPERIMENTS:  5.1 SYNTHETIC DATA AND PERFORMANCE MEASURES: We first evaluate and compare eVKF to other online variational methods as well as classic filtering methods using synthetic data. Since the ground truth is available for synthetic examples, we can measure the goodness of inferred latent states and learned dynamical system in reference to the true ones. To measure the filtering performance, we use the temporal average log density of inferred filtering distribution evaluated at the true state trajectory: T−1 ∑T t=1 log q(Zt;λ ∗ t ), where λ ∗ t are the optimal variational parameters of the approximation of the filtering distribution at time t. To assess the learning of the dynamics model, we sample points around the attractor manifold, evolve them one step forward, and calculate the KL divergence to the true dynamics: S−1 ∑S i=1 DKL ( pθ∗(zt+1 | Zit)||pθ(zt+1 | Zit) ) , where Zit are the perturbed samples around the attractor manifold (e.g. stable limit cycle) of the true dynamics, pθ∗ is the learned distribution over the dynamics, and pθ is the true distribution over the dynamics. This helps us evaluate the learned dynamics in the vicinity of the attractor where most samples originate from. The above divergence measures only the local structure of the learned dynamical system. To evaluate the long-term structure, we employ the Chamfer distance (Wu et al., 2021) DCD(S1||S2) = |S1|−1 ∑ x∈S1 min y∈S2 ||x− y||2 + |S2|−1 ∑ y∈S2 min x∈S1 ||y − x||2 (24) where S1 and S2 are two distinct sets of points. Usually, this metric is used to evaluate the similarity of point clouds. Intuitively, a low Chamfer distance would mean that trajectories from the learned dynamics would generate a manifold (point cloud) close to the true dynamics—a signature that the attractor structure can be generated. Since the Chamfer distance is not symmetric, we symmetrize it as DCD(S1, S2) = 12 (DCD(S1||S2) + DCD(S2||S1)) and take the logarithm. 5.1.1 CHAOTIC RECURRENT NEURAL NETWORK DYNAMICS: We first evaluate the filtering performance of eVKF. **Challenges and Considerations with NNs in eVKF:**

*   **Interpretability (Black Box Problem):** While the eVKF framework imposes a probabilistic structure on the latent states, the specific functions learned by the NNs (e.g., the non-linear transformations) remain largely uninterpretable. This makes it difficult to directly understand *why* the system transitioned in a certain way or *how* the latent state maps to observed activity at a mechanistic level. For neural dynamics, biological interpretability is often a key goal.
*   **Data Requirements:** Training complex NNs typically requires large amounts of data to prevent overfitting. Neural data, especially from single experimental sessions, can be limited, raising concerns about the robustness and generalizability of the learned models.
*   **Training Stability and Convergence:** Variational inference with NNs can be notoriously difficult to optimize. Issues like vanishing/exploding gradients, sensitivity to initialization, and hyperparameter tuning can impede training stability and lead to suboptimal local minima.
*   **Identifiability:** In complex non-linear state-space models, different sets of parameters can lead to observationally equivalent systems. This "identifiability crisis" means that even if the model fits the data well, the learned latent dynamics might not be unique or biologically meaningful. The eVKF framework needs mechanisms or assumptions to mitigate this.
*   **Computational Cost:** Training and inference with large neural networks can be computationally intensive, especially for long time series or large datasets.

**Overall Suitability in eVKF Context:**
The eVKF's strength lies in its attempt to marry the representational power of NNs with the principled probabilistic framework of state-space models. By explicitly modeling the latent states and their transitions, it offers more structure than a pure recurrent neural network (RNN) while being more flexible than a traditional EKF/UKF. The success hinges on whether this marriage effectively balances the expressivity of NNs with the interpretability and robustness derived from the probabilistic framework.

### 2. Assessment of Experimental Setup

#### 2.1. Synthetic Data Experiments

*   **Purpose:** Synthetic data is crucial for validating the eVKF's core functionality, robustness, and ability to recover ground truth.
*   **Ideal Setup:**
    *   **Known Ground Truth:** The generative process for the synthetic data should be precisely known, allowing for quantitative comparison of the learned latent states and dynamics parameters against the true ones.
    *   **Varying Complexity:** The synthetic dynamics should range from simple linear systems (where eVKF should reduce to or perform similarly to a Kalman Filter) to increasingly complex non-linear systems (e.g., Lorenz attractor, Chua's circuit, or a simulated network of spiking neurons with known connectivity). This tests the NN's ability to capture non-linearities.
    *   **Noise Characteristics:** Experimentation with varying levels and types of observation noise (Gaussian, Poisson for spikes, etc.) and process noise is essential to assess the filter's robustness and inference accuracy.
    *   **Dimensionality:** Testing with different latent and observation dimensions to ensure scalability.
    *   **Quantitative Metrics:** Beyond visual inspection, metrics like mean squared error (MSE) between true and inferred latent states (up to rotation/scaling), parameter recovery accuracy, and log-likelihood estimates are vital.
*   **Potential Critique Points:**
    *   **Oversimplification:** If the synthetic data is too simple (e.g., just linear dynamics with Gaussian noise), it may not adequately challenge the non-linear capabilities of the eVKF.
    *   **Limited Scenarios:** If only one type of non-linearity or noise characteristic is tested, the generality of the findings is limited.
    *   **Lack of Baselines:** Performance should be compared against simpler state-space models (KF, EKF, UKF, VRNN without Kalman-like structure) to highlight the specific advantages of the eVKF.

#### 2.2. Real-World Electrophysiological Data Experiments

*   **Data Type:** The paper should specify the exact type of electrophysiological data used (e.g., multi-electrode array recordings of spiking activity, local field potentials (LFPs), ECoG, EEG, MEG). Each has unique characteristics (sampling rate, signal-to-noise ratio, spatial/temporal resolution, underlying biophysics).
*   **Preprocessing:** This is critically important and often a weak point in papers.
    *   **Spiking Data:** Spike sorting quality, binning strategies (e.g., 10-20ms bins for population activity), smoothing (e.g., Gaussian kernel).
    *   **LFP/ECoG/EEG/MEG:** Filtering (band-pass), artifact removal (line noise, movement artifacts), common average referencing, normalization.
    *   **Dimensionality Reduction (Pre-eVKF):** Did they perform PCA or ICA before feeding into eVKF? If so, why, and how does it affect the eVKF's ability to learn representations? If not, how does eVKF handle the raw high-dimensional data?
*   **Experimental Paradigms:** The behavioral task associated with the neural data is vital for interpreting latent states. Is it a motor task (reaching, grasping), cognitive task (decision-making, memory), or passive observation? This informs what *kind* of dynamics one might expect.
*   **Comparison Baselines:** Crucial for demonstrating the eVKF's utility.
    *   **Traditional State-Space Models:** EKF, UKF, Linear Dynamical Systems (LDS).
    *   **Deep Learning Models:** Variational RNNs (VRNN), Recurrent VAEs, LFADS (Latent Factor Analysis via Dynamical Systems – a strong benchmark for neural data).
    *   **Other Dimensionality Reduction Techniques:** PCA, factor analysis, GP-LVM, t-SNE/UMAP (though these are not dynamic models).
*   **Performance Metrics:**
    *   **Reconstruction Accuracy:** How well does the model reconstruct the observed neural activity from the inferred latent states? (e.g., MSE, Pearson correlation).
    *   **Predictive Performance:** How well does the model predict future neural activity? (e.g., out-of-sample log-likelihood, predictive MSE).
    *   **Decoding Performance:** If a behavioral variable is available (e.g., arm kinematics, target location, choice), how well can it be decoded from the learned latent states compared to baselines? This is a strong indicator of a "useful" representation.
    *   **Smoothness/Continuity:** While often qualitative, the latent trajectories should appear smooth and continuous, reflecting biological continuity.
    *   **Temporal Resolution:** Does the model capture fine-grained or coarse-grained dynamics?

### 3. Analysis of Results on Real-World Data: Does eVKF Learn a Useful Latent Representation?

The "usefulness" of a latent representation is multifaceted and depends heavily on the scientific question.

*   **Evidence for Usefulness (What to look for in the results):**
    *   **Reduced Dimensionality with High Fidelity:** The eVKF should demonstrate that a low-dimensional latent space can capture a significant amount of variance in the high-dimensional neural activity, with reconstruction errors comparable to or better than state-of-the-art methods.
    *   **Smooth and Biologically Plausible Trajectories:** Visualizations of latent trajectories (e.g., 2D/3D projections) should show smooth, continuous flows rather than noisy, chaotic jumps. If the task has distinct phases (e.g., preparation, movement, hold), these should ideally separate in the latent space.
    *   **Decodability of External Variables:** This is often the strongest empirical evidence of usefulness. If the latent states allow for superior decoding of motor kinematics, behavioral choices, or cognitive states compared to using raw neural data or representations from other models, it strongly suggests the eVKF has extracted salient information.
    *   **Separation of Conditions/States:** If the task involves different conditions (e.g., different movement directions, different stimuli), do the latent trajectories corresponding to these conditions separate distinctly in the latent space? This indicates that the latent space encodes task-relevant information.
    *   **Generalizability Across Sessions/Subjects:** A truly useful representation should generalize to new, unseen data from the same subject or ideally, across different subjects (if a common space is learned or if the model can be fine-tuned easily).
    *   **Discovery of Novel Dynamics:** In the best-case scenario, the eVKF might reveal previously unobserved dynamic features or relationships between neurons that provide new insights into neural computation. For example, specific oscillatory patterns or transient dynamics related to specific events.
    *   **Comparison to LFADS:** LFADS has set a high bar for inferring latent dynamics from spiking data. If eVKF can match or surpass LFADS in terms of reconstruction, prediction, and decoding, especially on spike train data, it would be a significant achievement.

*   **Potential Weaknesses in Demonstrating Usefulness:**
    *   **Focus on Reconstruction Only:** If the paper primarily focuses on reconstruction error, it doesn't fully prove the *interpretability* or *utility* of the latent space for downstream tasks. A model could perfectly reconstruct the data but have a completely jumbled or uninterpretable latent space.
    *   **Lack of Causal Links:** While the model might capture correlations, it does not inherently reveal causal relationships. The paper should be cautious about implying causality from learned dynamics.
    *   **Overfitting to Specific Tasks/Subjects:** If the model performs well only on one specific dataset or subject and fails to generalize, its utility is limited.
    *   **Ambiguous Interpretations:** If the authors attempt to interpret latent dimensions but provide only vague or speculative connections to biology without strong empirical support (e.g., "latent dim 1 seems related to speed"), it weakens the claim of usefulness.

### 4. Critique of Experimental Design and Interpretation of Results

*   **Clarity of Model Components:** While I'm inferring the eVKF structure, the paper needs to explicitly detail which components are implemented by NNs (e.g., transition function, emission function, recognition network) and their specific architectures (MLP, RNN type, number of layers, units).
*   **Hyperparameter Tuning:** A major challenge with NN-based models. How were hyperparameters (learning rate, network sizes, regularization, noise variances) chosen? Was there a systematic search, cross-validation, or just ad-hoc tuning? Sensitivity analysis to hyperparameters is crucial.
*   **Statistical Rigor:** Were statistical tests performed for comparisons between eVKF and baselines? Are error bars provided for metrics? Are there enough trials/sessions/subjects to make generalizable claims?
*   **Ablation Studies:** To truly understand the contribution of each component of eVKF, ablation studies are essential. For example:
    *   What if the NN in the transition function is replaced by a linear model?
    *   What if the NN in the emission function is simplified?
    *   What if the Kalman-like filtering structure is removed, reducing it to a pure VRNN?
    *   This helps isolate the specific benefits of the "eVKF" part versus just using NNs.
*   **Computational Efficiency:** How long does training take? Can the model perform real-time inference? This is critical for practical applications like brain-computer interfaces.
*   **Limitations and Future Work:** A strong paper acknowledges its limitations.
    *   Are there theoretical guarantees for convergence or identifiability?
    *   What are the computational bottlenecks?
    *   How does it handle non-stationarity in neural data?
    *   What about incorporating external inputs (e.g., stimuli, motor commands) into the dynamics?
*   **Biological Interpretation vs. Pure Modeling:** The paper should clearly state its primary goal. Is it to provide a highly accurate predictive model, or to extract biologically meaningful insights? If the latter, more effort should be spent on interpreting the learned dynamics in the context of neuroscience.
*   **Reproducibility:** Are implementation details (code availability, specific library versions, random seeds) sufficiently provided to allow for independent reproduction of results?

**Conclusion:**

The eVKF algorithm, as conceptually outlined, represents a promising direction for modeling complex neural dynamics by synergistically combining neural networks with principled probabilistic inference. Its strength lies in its potential to capture non-linearities and high-dimensional observations while retaining a structured latent space.

However, a thorough evaluation hinges on robust experimental design. The synthetic data experiments must rigorously test the model's ability to recover known ground truth across varying complexities and noise levels. On real-world electrophysiological data, the paper must demonstrate clear and quantitative advantages over state-of-the-art baselines across multiple metrics (reconstruction, prediction, and especially decoding of behavior/cognitive states). The "usefulness" of the latent representation must be empirically demonstrated, not just visually suggested.   "output": "This detailed review will assess the eVKF algorithm from the perspective of an expert in online learning algorithms, focusing on its efficiency, scalability, and suitability for real-time applications.

Assuming "eVKF" refers to an Ensemble Variational Kalman Filter or a similar ensemble-based variational inference approach for state estimation in dynamic systems, let's proceed with the review.

---

### **Review of the eVKF Algorithm for Online Learning**

The proposed eVKF algorithm positions itself as an online learning method for state estimation, likely in the context of dynamic systems. Its core promise lies in leveraging the benefits of ensemble methods for scalability while aiming for the more robust uncertainty quantification offered by variational inference.

#### **1. Online Learning Aspects & Real-Time Capability**

*   **Inherent Online Nature:** The eVKF, by design, operates as a sequential filter. It processes observations one at a time, performing a prediction (forecast) step and an update (analysis) step at each time instance. This sequential processing, where past data is not revisited (unless using a smoother, which is typically offline), is the hallmark of an online learning algorithm. The state posterior distribution (or an approximation thereof) is updated incrementally as new data arrives.
*   **Definition of "Learning":** In the context of eVKF, "learning" primarily refers to the *online estimation of the system's hidden state variables* and their associated uncertainties. If the algorithm also simultaneously estimates or adapts model parameters (e.g., process noise, measurement noise covariances, or even system dynamics parameters), then it constitutes true online parameter learning, which would significantly enhance its adaptability. Most filter algorithms, including basic Kalman filters and their ensemble variants, primarily perform state estimation assuming fixed model parameters. If eVKF incorporates adaptive mechanisms for these parameters, it would be a significant strength.
*   **Real-time Suitability:**
    *   **Parallelizability:** Like other ensemble-based methods (e.g., EnKF), the prediction step, where each ensemble member is propagated independently through the system dynamics, is highly parallelizable. This is a crucial advantage for real-time applications on multi-core processors or GPUs.
    *   **Iterative Nature of Variational Inference:** The core of eVKF involves a variational inference (VI) step during the update phase. VI often requires an iterative optimization procedure (e.g., coordinate ascent, gradient descent on the ELBO). The *number of iterations (K)* for this internal optimization is critical for real-time performance. If K is large or if the convergence is slow, the per-step computational cost can become prohibitive, jeopardizing real-time deadlines.
    *   **Fixed-Time Budget:** For real-time applications, the algorithm must complete its computations within a fixed time budget between observations. The eVKF's ability to meet this budget depends on the product of the ensemble size (N) and the cost of the iterative VI step.

#### **2. Computational Complexity Analysis**

Let $N$ be the ensemble size, $D_x$ be the state dimension, and $D_z$ be the observation dimension. Let $K$ be the number of internal variational iterations.

*   **Prediction Step:** Similar to EnKF, this involves propagating $N$ ensemble members through the system dynamics. If the dynamics model is computationally expensive, this will be the dominant cost. Typically, it's $O(N \cdot \text{cost_of_dynamics_model})$. If the model is linear, this is $O(N \cdot D_x^2)$.
*   **Analysis (Update) Step:** This is where eVKF significantly differs and adds complexity.
    *   **Ensemble Covariance Calculation:** Calculation of sample covariances ($P_f, H P_f H^T$) involves operations like $O(N \cdot D_x^2)$ or $O(N \cdot D_z^2)$.
    *   **Variational Inference Iterations:** This is the most complex part. Each iteration usually involves:
        *   Matrix inversions or linear system solves: Typically $O(D_z^3)$ or $O(D_x^3)$ depending on the specific variational family and update equations.
        *   Matrix multiplications: $O(D_x^2 \cdot D_z)$, $O(D_x \cdot D_z^2)$, etc.
        *   Calculations involving all $N$ ensemble members: $O(N \cdot D_x)$, $O(N \cdot D_z)$.
    *   Therefore, the analysis step complexity is roughly $O(K \cdot (D_z^3 + D_x^3 + N \cdot D_x \cdot D_z))$.
*   **Overall Complexity:** The per-time-step complexity of eVKF is approximately $O(N \cdot \text{cost_of_dynamics} + K \cdot (D_x^3 + D_z^3 + N \cdot D_x \cdot D_z))$. This is significantly more complex than the basic EnKF or BPF due to the iterative $K$ factor and the cubic terms in $D_x, D_z$.

#### **3. Comparison to Other Online Methods**

*   **Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF):**
    *   **Computational Cost:** Dominantly $O(N \cdot D_x^2)$ for linear systems, or $O(N \cdot \text{cost_of_dynamics})$ + $O(N \cdot D_x^2 + N \cdot D_z^2)$ for the update. It avoids explicit covariance matrix calculations for the state, making it scalable to high $D_x$. It typically has *no internal iterations* in its standard form.
    *   **Accuracy:** Good for systems that are "mildly" non-linear or where the Gaussian approximation for the posterior is reasonable. Can suffer from filter divergence, particularly if the ensemble size is too small or if the effective gain is poor (e.g., due to linearizations). Tends to underestimate uncertainty.
    *   **eVKF vs. EnKF:** eVKF is *computationally more expensive per time step* due to the iterative VI step. However, eVKF *aims for higher accuracy* by performing a more sophisticated (and often more robust) approximation of the posterior distribution via variational inference. This may lead to better uncertainty quantification and potentially more stable estimates, especially for highly non-Gaussian posteriors or when the linearized update of EnKF is problematic. The hope is that eVKF might achieve comparable accuracy with a *smaller ensemble size (N)* than EnKF, thus potentially balancing the overall cost. This trade-off needs rigorous empirical validation.

*   **Bootstrap Particle Filter (BPF):**
    *   **Computational Cost:** $O(N \cdot \text{cost_of_dynamics}) + O(N \cdot D_z + N \log N)$ (for resampling). It does not involve high-dimensional matrix operations explicitly.
    *   **Accuracy:** Conceptually the most general, capable of representing *arbitrary* non-linear and non-Gaussian distributions if given enough particles. Provides a direct Monte Carlo approximation of the posterior.
    *   **eVKF vs. BPF:** BPF struggles significantly with high-dimensional state spaces ($D_x \gg 1$) due to the "curse of dimensionality," requiring an exponentially growing number of particles ($N$) to maintain accuracy. This makes it computationally prohibitive for many practical applications unless advanced proposal distributions are used (e.g., using Kalman filters for proposal, which introduces its own complexity). eVKF, by assuming a structured (e.g., Gaussian) variational family, aims to overcome the dimensionality issue of BPF while still handling non-linearities better than EnKF. It is likely to be *more computationally efficient than BPF for high-dimensional problems* for a given accuracy, as it might require significantly fewer particles $N$. However, eVKF's accuracy is bounded by its chosen variational family, whereas BPF is theoretically exact with infinite particles.

#### **4. Accuracy-Computational Cost Trade-offs**

The eVKF algorithm presents a clear trade-off space, particularly relevant for real-time applications:

*   **Ensemble Size (N):** A larger N generally leads to a more accurate representation of the ensemble moments (mean, covariance) and a better approximation of the posterior, but directly increases computational cost.
*   **Number of Variational Iterations (K):** A larger K allows the variational approximation to converge closer to the optimal solution within the chosen family, potentially leading to higher accuracy in the posterior mean and covariance. However, increasing K directly increases the per-step computational cost.
*   **The Sweet Spot:** The challenge for eVKF in real-time is to find the *minimum combination of N and K* that satisfies the required accuracy level *and* completes within the available time budget. If the algorithm requires large N and/or large K to achieve competitive accuracy, its real-time applicability will be limited.
*   **Uncertainty Quantification:** A key potential advantage of eVKF is better uncertainty quantification compared to EnKF. This means the filter provides more reliable estimates of the posterior variance/covariance, which is crucial for decision-making and downstream control tasks. Achieving this improved uncertainty with manageable computational cost is the primary trade-off being sought.

#### **5. Critique of Online Learning Implementation**

*   **Robustness of Variational Optimization:** The iterative VI step is central. How robust is its convergence in real-time settings? Does it always converge within K iterations? What happens if it doesn't? Are there guarantees for convergence? The choice of a fixed K might be computationally predictable but might sacrifice accuracy if the system state is in a challenging region, or waste computation if convergence is fast. A dynamic stopping criterion based on ELBO convergence (e.g., when change in ELBO is below a threshold) would be more efficient but adds complexity.
*   **Scalability for High Dimensions:** While ensemble methods are generally good for high-dimensional states, the $D_x^3$ and $D_z^3$ terms in the VI step's complexity can still become a bottleneck for very high-dimensional problems. Are there specific approximations or linear algebra tricks employed to mitigate this for large $D_x$ or $D_z$?
*   **Handling of Non-Gaussianities:** eVKF uses variational inference, often assuming a Gaussian (or other simple) family for the approximate posterior. While this is better than EnKF's simpler update, it's still an approximation. How well does it handle highly multi-modal or significantly non-Gaussian posteriors that might arise in highly non-linear systems?
*   **Parameter Adaptation:** A critical aspect of "learning" is adaptability. Does eVKF incorporate online learning of unknown or time-varying noise covariances or model parameters? Without this, its adaptability to changing real-world conditions is limited, and its performance would depend heavily on correctly specified prior parameters.
*   **Initialization Strategy:** How are the initial ensemble and the variational parameters initialized? In an online setting, a robust and quick initialization scheme is essential, especially when starting from scratch or recovering from significant sensor outages.
*   **Numerical Stability:** Iterative optimization algorithms can be prone to numerical instability, especially in floating-point arithmetic. Are measures taken to ensure stability (e.g., regularization, Cholesky decomposition for positive definiteness)?

#### **6. Critique of Performance Evaluation**

*   **Computational Cost Measurement:**
    *   **Wall-Clock Time:** Crucial for real-time. Simply stating Big-O complexity is insufficient. Actual runtimes on representative hardware for different $N, D_x, D_z, K$ values are necessary.
    *   **Scalability Plots:** Showing how wall-clock time scales with increasing $N, D_x, D_z$ for eVKF, EnKF, and BPF would clearly demonstrate their real-time applicability limits.
    *   **Fair Comparison:** When comparing eVKF, EnKF, and BPF, it's vital to compare them at *equivalent accuracy levels* rather than fixed $N$. For example, find the minimum $N$ (and $K$ for eVKF) for each algorithm to achieve a target RMSE, then compare their associated computational costs. This reveals the true "efficiency" trade-off.
*   **Metrics for Accuracy:**
    *   **RMSE/MAE:** Standard for state mean estimation.
    *   **Uncertainty Quantification Metrics:** Given eVKF's claim of better uncertainty, metrics beyond point estimates are crucial. Examples include:
        *   **Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL):** Measures how well the estimated distribution matches the true state.
        *   **Coverage Probability:** For 95% credible intervals, how often does the true state fall within the estimated interval? (Should be close to 95%).
        *   **Credibility Interval Width/Volume:** How tight are the uncertainty estimates?
        *   **Mahalanobis Distance:** How well does the true state fit within the estimated covariance ellipsoid?
*   **Benchmark Scenarios:**
    *   **Non-linearity and Non-Gaussianity:** The test cases should adequately challenge the linear and Gaussian assumptions of EnKF and demonstrate where eVKF excels. Cases with multi-modal posteriors would be particularly revealing.
    *   **Dimensionality Range:** Evaluate performance across a range of $D_x$ and $D_z$ to demonstrate scalability.
    *   **Real-world Data:** While synthetic data allows for ground truth, demonstrating performance on real-world datasets with their inherent complexities (outliers, missing data, model mismatch) is essential for real-time applications.
    *   **Long-Term Performance:** How does the filter perform over extended periods? Does it maintain stability or diverge?
*   **Sensitivity Analysis:** How sensitive is eVKF's performance (both accuracy and speed) to the choice of $N$ and $K$? This informs users on how to tune the algorithm for their specific real-time constraints.
*   **Reproducibility:** Detailed descriptions of simulation environments, hyperparameter settings, and random seeds are crucial for reproducibility.

---

### **Conclusion and Recommendations for Real-time Applications**

The eVKF algorithm represents a promising direction for online state estimation, attempting to strike a balance between the efficiency of ensemble methods and the robustness of variational inference.

**Strengths for Online Learning / Real-time:**
*   Inherently sequential processing.
*   Parallelizable prediction step.
*   Potential for better uncertainty quantification than EnKF.
*   Potential to handle higher dimensions than BPF for similar accuracy.

**Weaknesses / Areas for Improvement for Real-time:**
*   Higher per-step computational cost than EnKF due to iterative VI.
*   Dependence on the number of variational iterations ($K$) for convergence and real-time budget.
*   Potential scalability issues with very high $D_x$ or $D_z$ if cubic terms dominate.
*   Need for robust and efficient VI optimization, particularly with dynamic stopping criteria.
*   Limited by the choice of variational family (e.g., Gaussian approximation).

**Recommendations:**
1.  **Emphasize Empirical Computational Cost:** Provide comprehensive benchmarks showing wall-clock times across different $N, D_x, D_z, K$ for eVKF, EnKF, and BPF.
2.  **Accuracy-Efficiency Frontier:** Present plots showing the trade-off between RMSE (and NLL/coverage) and computational cost for varying $N$ and $K$ for all compared algorithms. This will highlight where eVKF offers the best value proposition.
3.  **Dynamic K:** Investigate and implement dynamic stopping criteria for the variational iterations to optimize computational cost without sacrificing too much accuracy, which is vital for meeting real-time deadlines.
4.  **Adaptive Parameters:** Explore extensions of eVKF to learn or adapt noise covariances or system model parameters online. This would significantly enhance its "learning" capabilities and robustness in real-world scenarios.
5.  **Benchmarking against Advanced PFs:** Compare against more advanced Particle Filter variants (e.g., Ensemble PFs, Gaussian Mixture Model PFs) or other non-linear filters to fully contextualize its performance.

In summary, eVKF has the potential to be a strong contender for online learning in real-time systems where both state estimation accuracy and robust uncertainty quantification are critical. However, its practical adoption will heavily depend on its demonstrated ability to consistently meet computational deadlines, which requires a rigorous analysis of its inherent iterative costs and careful empirical validation against leading online filtering methods.",

    *   **Critique:** This is a crucial assumption. The choice of $q(z_t)$ dictates the complexity and accuracy of the approximation. For instance, if $q(z_t)$ is chosen as a Gaussian (which is an exponential family), it naturally handles modes and variance but may fail to capture multi-modality or strong non-Gaussian features of the true posterior. The success relies on the true posterior *being well-approximated* by the chosen exponential family. The paper should clearly justify *why* this specific family is appropriate for the types of state-space models it aims to solve.
